terms.definition: Coaches' game film shot so that all 22 players on the field can be seen at the same time, instead of the broadcast view that follows the ball.
A receiver who will not extend his arms for a catch for fear of contact; also called T-rex arms.
A lineman's ability to stand his ground and not be moved back, especially against a bull rush.
Throwing or reacting before the play shows itself, such as a quarterback releasing the ball before the receiver comes out of his break.
A quarterback's overall throwing ability: arm strength, quick release, accuracy, touch and the ability to throw from different platforms.
Putting the pass where only the receiver can get it and where he can keep running, such as the outside shoulder or in stride.
A defender's or receiver's ability to find, track and play the ball in the air, including high-pointing and making interceptions or catches.
The ability to flex the ankles, knees and hips so a player can stay low, keep leverage and turn the corner; linemen bend at the knees rather than the waist.
A receiver who traps the ball against his body instead of catching it with his hands.
Scouts' word for a prospect's rear end; a big bubble means a powerful lower body.
A quarterback who pats the ball too long before throwing, so a defensive back jumps the route.
Sudden acceleration from a standing start or a cut, the speed that closes the gap.
A drafted player, usually a high pick, who fails to meet the expectations of the team that drafted him.
A prospect or player with no long-term NFL future who fills out a training camp roster.
A defender who lets the ball carrier run into him and hopes he goes down, instead of striking through him.
The best level a prospect could realistically reach if he develops fully; a high ceiling usually means he is not yet a finished player. Also called upside.
A player's ability to switch directions sharply without losing balance or speed; the 3-cone and shuttle drills test it.
A catch-all for a prospect's off-field conduct and personal qualities, which teams research before the draft.
A defensive back's ability to plant, change direction and rapidly close on the ball.
How well a player accepts and applies coaching.
The league panel that gives underclassmen a free evaluation: a first-round grade, a second-round grade, or advice to stay in school.
The medical and injury exam every combine invitee goes through, which teams treat as the most important part of the event.
A runner's ability to stay on his feet and keep moving after being hit.
A catch made while a defender is in position to break it up; scouts rate how often a receiver wins these.
Slang for a player with poor balance and clumsy, awkward footwork.
A very large lineman who moves with surprising agility and good feet.
A rookie advanced enough in technique or talent to start from his first season (also called plug and play).
A college underclassman's formal notice that he is entering the NFL draft, which ends his remaining college eligibility.
A back who attacks upfield quickly with forward lean and no sideways hesitation (north-south runner).
How likely a player is to stay healthy and available; scouts and coaches mark injury-prone players down.
A college player who enters the NFL draft before using up his college eligibility, with league approval.
A top speed or burst a player shows only when he needs it, so he pulls away from coverage after seeming to have reached his limit.
Where a quarterback or defender looks; quarterbacks use their eyes to read the field or to manipulate safeties, and keeping eyes up under pressure is a plus.
How quick and how correct a player's first move is after the snap or after seeing the play.
How freely a player's joints move; scouts look for loose hips and knee bend, and stiffness shows up as linear or tight movement.
The least a team can reasonably expect from a prospect; a high floor means a safe pick who is unlikely to flop.
How well a player understands the game and applies it: reading plays, processing quickly, adjusting. Often grouped with instincts and the word cerebral.
How a player's feet move and set, such as a quarterback's drops and balance or a lineman's steps and base.
A prospect whose athleticism is far beyond what is normal for his position.
Strength that shows up on the field, as opposed to weight-room numbers such as combine bench reps.
A quarterback who makes few mistakes for a team that relies on its defense and running game to win.
Slang for an offensive lineman who plays with a relentless, vicious mentality; 'needs some glass in his diet' means he plays soft.
A scout's or team's rating of a prospect, either a numeric score on his traits or a tier that says where he should be drafted (for example a first-round grade).
Where a blocker or defender puts his hands on the opponent; blockers want them inside the defender's shoulders.
How well a lineman or defender uses his hands: timing, placement and strength of strikes, grabs and sheds.
A receiver who extends his arms and catches the ball away from his body with his hands.
Catching or breaking up a pass at its highest reachable point, usually with a jump, above the defender.
Loose, flexible hips that let a player turn and change direction smoothly without losing speed; the opposite is stiff or tight hips.
terms.variants: fluid hips; oily hips; tight hips (opposite); linear (Defector's opposite)

terms.definition: A natural feel for where the play is going and how to react to it quickly.
A prospect's non-physical qualities such as leadership, toughness, work habits and competitiveness.
A stand-up end or strong-side linebacker who rushes the passer; Fox also notes it can describe a tight end as a moveable chess piece.
An ordinary player with no standout trait, not expected to be more than average at his level.
Long arms and overall reach for his position; teams measure arm length and prize it in pass rushers, tackles and cornerbacks.
Top running speed over a long distance (straight-line speed), as opposed to quickness over a few steps.
The numbers recorded at the combine and pro days: height, weight, arm length, hand size, and times and jumps.
How hard and how long a player keeps playing at full effort on every snap.
A player with limited athleticism who is productive through work ethic and intangibles; the underachiever has more talent than output.

aliases: plays with his pads too high
terms.definition: How low a player keeps his shoulder pads; staying low wins leverage and playing too upright loses it.
A back's ability to block rushers and pick up blitzes to protect the quarterback.
An offensive lineman with below-average feet who is effective only in tight spaces.
How fast a player looks in real game action compared with his timed speed (plays faster than his 40 time).

terms.term: Plays until he hears glass break
terms.definition: A phrase for a player who keeps playing until the whistle.
A quarterback's feel for pressure that lets him move within the pocket, step up or slide, and keep his eyes downfield.
How quickly a player takes in what he sees, recognizes it and reacts; for quarterbacks it covers reading the defense before and after the snap.
What a player actually did in games (statistics and results), as opposed to physical traits and testing numbers.
A lineman's quick strike with both hands into the opponent's chest to stop his charge or move him back.
A player who is sharp in short areas but lacks long-distance speed (the opposite is a straight-line runner).
Reading the keys of a developing play, diagnosing it and reacting; also called keying and diagnosing.
How quickly a defensive back closes back on the ball or receiver after falling behind.
A 0 to 10 score of how a prospect's combine or pro day measurements compare with others at his position since 1987.
How a receiver gets off the line of scrimmage, especially against press coverage; usually just called his release.
A college underclassman's decision not to declare and to play another college season.
A lineman who drives defenders off the ball in the running game.
A receiver's skill at running precise routes, selling fakes and making sharp breaks to get open.
A defensive back's or safety's willingness and ability to come up and help stop the run.
How well a player's skills match the blocking, coverage or other system a particular team runs.
The space a receiver gets between himself and the defender covering him.
How fast a player can accelerate and change direction in a few yards, which matters more for linemen and slot players than 40-yard speed.
A prospect who is expected to be picked later than his ability deserves, or who gets little attention but may outplay his draft slot.
A skill player who excels in open areas through speed and athleticism.

League approval for a player who is not yet draft-eligible under the normal rule, such as an underclassman petitioning to enter; the player must meet the three-year rule and give up his college eligibility.
A metric for running backs that scales 40-yard time by weight, using (weight x 200) / (40 time to the fourth power); a heavy back with a fast time scores high.
The recorded video of a player's games that scouts and coaches study to judge him; 'film' is the older word and means the same.
A prospect must be at least three years out of high school to be eligible for the NFL draft.
A thin, wiry player who may struggle to add muscle and size; generally a negative.
A quarterback's ability to vary the speed and trajectory of a pass so it drops softly over or between defenders.
The individual physical and mental qualities scouts grade a prospect on (arm strength, footwork, speed, instincts), as distinct from his game results.
A player whose size or skills fall between two positions, so teams are unsure where he fits (for example too light for end and too slow for linebacker).
Describes sudden quickness and explosive movement in all directions (quick twitch).
How fast the quarterback's pass travels when it arrives, as distinct from how far he can throw it.
A runner's ability to see daylight and cut to open lanes; for receivers, Bleacher Report uses it for finding and tracking the ball.
An offensive or defensive lineman who bends at the waist instead of the knees and so loses balance and leverage.
A tackler who briefly sticks to the ball carrier then slides off.
How hard a player prepares and trains, judged from tape, coaches and references.
A prospect whose draft stock rises on strong combine testing despite an average or poor college career.
A receiver's or back's ability to gain yards after the catch by speed, agility and breaking tackles.
